title: Looking at Real Cells
colour_map: Reuses the first film's map. Cell wall TAN, membrane thin BLUE line, large central vacuole PALE BLUE, nucleus PURPLE, mitochondria ORANGE, chloroplasts GREEN, light YELLOW. Microscope views are labelled cartoons marked 'schematic', not photographs and not to the same scale: in them, stain tints are shown as a class would see them (iodine: pale yellow-brown cells with darker nuclei; methylene blue: blue cells) but every wall is outlined TAN and every nucleus ringed PURPLE so the parts match the first film. Every number appears only as on-screen text.

scenes.visual: Title card 'Looking at Real Cells' over a school light microscope drawn in simple lines, its round circle of light glowing.

scenes.tts: Everything in the first film was a drawing: a kit, a box and a water tank. How do we know a real plant cell has a box? And how big is one?
scenes.visual: The first film's boxy celery cell (TAN wall, PALE BLUE tank, GREEN chloroplasts) sits on a sheet of paper with a pencil beside it, stamp 'drawing'. Two question cards pop up: 'a real box?' and 'how big?'.
scenes.narration: Everything in the first film was a drawing: a kit, a box and a water tank. How do we know a real plant cell has a box? And how big is one?

scenes.tts: A real celery cell is too small to see with your eyes alone. To check the model's parts, you need a light microscope and a way to measure.
scenes.visual: A celery stalk next to a magnifier icon; zooming in shows only a blur, label 'too small to see'. The microscope slides in from the right. Two tool icons appear below it: a lens ('look') and a ruler ('measure').
scenes.narration: A real celery cell is too small to see with your eyes alone. To check the model's parts, you need a light microscope and a way to measure.

scenes.tts: First, make a wet mount. A thin piece of onion skin sits in a drop of iodine stain, under a thin glass cover slip.
scenes.visual: Hands in gloves peel a see-through layer from inside a cut onion bulb with tweezers, lay it on a glass slide, add a drop of yellow-brown iodine, and lower a square cover slip at an angle. Labels: 'onion skin', 'iodine stain', 'cover slip'.
scenes.narration: First, make a wet mount. A thin piece of onion skin sits in a drop of iodine stain, under a thin glass cover slip.

scenes.tts: Light passes up through the thin layer. Through the eyepiece, you see a round circle of light.
scenes.visual: Side view of the microscope: a YELLOW beam rises from the lamp through the slide and the lenses to an eye. Cut to the eyepiece view: a bright round circle on black, label 'circle of light'.
scenes.narration: Light passes up through the thin layer. Through the eyepiece, you see a round circle of light.

scenes.tts: Inside it, onion skin cells sit side by side, like long boxes. The stain makes each nucleus look darker.
scenes.visual: Schematic onion view fills the circle: long rectangular cells in a brick-like pattern, pale yellow-brown, each outlined TAN, each with one darker dot ringed PURPLE. Labels 'wall' and 'nucleus' with leader lines. Label 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Inside it, onion skin cells sit side by side, like long boxes. The stain makes each nucleus look darker.

scenes.tts: Notice what is missing. These onion cells are not green. They have walls, but no developed chloroplasts.
scenes.visual: A GREEN chloroplast icon floats over the onion view and searches across it, then fades with a GREY dash, label 'no chloroplasts seen'. The TAN walls pulse once.
scenes.narration: Notice what is missing. These onion cells are not green. They have walls, but no developed chloroplasts.

scenes.tts: Now a waterweed leaf, mounted in a drop of water. Its cells are boxy too, and most are packed with green chloroplasts.
scenes.visual: Slide swap: a small waterweed sprig, one leaf pulled off and laid in a water drop. Circle view: shorter boxy cells outlined TAN, each crowded with GREEN ovals. On-screen text 'tens to hundreds per cell'. Label 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Now a waterweed leaf, mounted in a drop of water. Its cells are boxy too, and most are packed with green chloroplasts.

scenes.tts: Last, a few cells from the inside of a cheek, colored with a blue stain. They have no box. They are thin and flat, like tiles on a floor.
scenes.visual: A drop of blue stain on a slide; circle view shows loose, flat, irregular rounded cells, tinted blue, each with a nucleus ringed PURPLE and only a thin BLUE outline, no TAN outline. A few overlap like scattered floor tiles. Small text: 'outline only; the membrane itself is too thin to see'. Label 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Last, a few cells from the inside of a cheek, colored with a blue stain. They have no box. They are thin and flat, like tiles on a floor.

scenes.tts: So the box is real. The plant cells show straight walls. The cheek cells show only a thin outline, with no wall.
scenes.visual: The three circle views shrink into a row: onion, waterweed, cheek. TAN walls glow in the first two; the cheek view shows a BLUE edge only. A tick appears beside 'a real box?' from the opening. Small text: 'circles not drawn to the same scale'.
scenes.narration: So the box is real. The plant cells show straight walls. The cheek cells show only a thin outline, with no wall.

scenes.tts: Now, how big? Scientists measure cells in micrometres. The screen shows how small one micrometre is.
scenes.visual: A millimetre ruler; one millimetre gap zooms open and splits into a thousand thin slices; one slice glows, label '1 micrometre (µm) = 1/1000 mm'.
scenes.narration: Now, how big? Scientists measure cells in micrometres. The screen shows how small one micrometre is.

scenes.tts: Scientists use a tiny ruler inside the eyepiece. In class, you can use the circle of light itself. Count similar cells lying end to end across it. Then divide the circle's width by that count. That gives a rough average width for one cell.
scenes.visual: Circle view with a thin scale line inside the eyepiece, label 'eyepiece ruler'. It fades; a GREY double arrow spans the circle's full width, label 'circle width'. Small numbered tags 1, 2, 3 drop onto similar cells lying end to end across it. Rule on screen: 'average cell width ≈ circle width ÷ number of cells'.
scenes.narration: Scientists use a tiny ruler inside the eyepiece. In class, you can use the circle of light itself. Count similar cells lying end to end across it. Then divide the circle's width by that count. That gives a rough average width for one cell.

scenes.tts: Try a made-up class example with cheek cells. The circle's width and the cell count are on the screen. About how wide is one cell?
scenes.visual: Circle view of blue cheek cells; the double arrow labelled '450 µm'; eight cheek cells lying end to end across it, tagged 1 to 8. Card: 'made-up numbers for practice'. Question: 'one cell ≈ ? µm'.
scenes.narration: Try a made-up class example with cheek cells. The circle's width and the cell count are on the screen. About how wide is one cell?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. Question card '450 µm across, 8 cells: one cell ≈ ? µm' holds; 5-second ring timer at bottom right.

scenes.tts: Divide, and the answer is on the screen. One published study measured cheek cells at nearly the same width. A rough count lands close.
scenes.visual: On screen: '450 ÷ 8 ≈ 56 µm'. Beside it a small card: 'published study: about 55 µm across'. The two numbers slide next to each other with an 'about the same' sign. A tick appears beside 'how big?'.
scenes.narration: Divide, and the answer is on the screen. One published study measured cheek cells at nearly the same width. A rough count lands close.

scenes.tts: One more surprise. Scientists found small clusters of colorless cells inside green waterweed leaves. These cells had no chloroplasts.
scenes.visual: Back to the waterweed circle view: among the GREEN-packed cells, a small cluster of cells with no GREEN ovals, outlined TAN, label 'colorless cells'. Caption card: 'Hara and colleagues, 2015'. Label 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: One more surprise. Scientists found small clusters of colorless cells inside green waterweed leaves. These cells had no chloroplasts.

scenes.tts: A dye still lit up a large central vacuole inside them. So even in one green leaf, not every plant cell is green.
scenes.visual: A dye wash passes over the slide; inside each colorless cell a big PALE BLUE tank lights up, matching the first film's water tank colour. Label 'large central vacuole'.
scenes.narration: A dye still lit up a large central vacuole inside them. So even in one green leaf, not every plant cell is green.

scenes.tts: Look and measure. The box is real, and so are the green chloroplasts and the water tank. But only some plant cells are green, and cells come in many shapes and sizes.
scenes.visual: The three circle views return in a row with the colorless waterweed cluster added as a fourth. The first film's celery drawing fades in above them with a dashed line from each of its parts (box, chloroplasts, tank) to where that part shows in a real view, label 'model's parts seen'. Under the row, simple outline icons of a long box, a short box and a flat tile, label 'many shapes and sizes'.
scenes.narration: Look and measure. The box is real, and so are the green chloroplasts and the water tank. But only some plant cells are green, and cells come in many shapes and sizes.

scenes.visual: End card with Hex mascot peering into a microscope. Line: 'Under the microscope, plant cells show their box; only some are green.'
